NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS SUMMIT MEETING IN MEXICO-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today the citizens and governments of more than one hundred nations, including Canada, will observe the first World Food Day, which will serve as a rallying point in the search for solutions to end world hunger and poverty. The natural right of all human beings to food was backed by the report of the parliamentary task force on North-South relations, which placed particular emphasis on food and agricultural production. The report was supported by all parties in the House and its main thrusts were endorsed by the government.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith):
That this House affirms its desire that practical steps be discussed by the heads of state or government of 22 countries who will meet next week for the historic North-South Summit in Mexico, so that early progress can be made in negotiating the economic issues now dividing North from South and, further, that the text of this motion be sent to the governments of all 22 states.

speechtext:

Whereas on a relative basis the people of Poland during World War II suffered as great a loss of both life and property as any other nation in that catastrophic conflict, and whereas following

an energy price agreement with the province of Alberta is to bring about a settlement which has placed less of a burden on the consumers of Canada than he would have permitted as a member of the former Government of Canada.

Madam Speaker,
I can play with figures the same way as the minister can play with figures. The point is that the prices for energy have risen 46 per cent to 55 per cent. My supplementary question concerns farmers. The farmers have been hit not only by high energy prices which affect their fuel costs, as well as costs of their fertilizer made from natural gas, but also by interest rates. Obviously this will mean higher food prices to all Canadians.
Why, in his 18 months in office, has the minister failed to address this issue, an issue which will cause countless Canadians to stretch their food budgets tighter and tighter and make it much more difficult to live in the country?

subsubtopic: UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my questions have to do with a growing nightmare for many tens of thousands of Canadian home owners who have urea formaldehyde foam insulation, and who are victims of one arm of government not knowing what the other arm is doing. We now have at least two different cabinet ministers saying two different things, and the others are running for cover.
I want to ask the President of the Treasury Board if he authorized his then parliamentary secretary, now the Minister of State without portofolio, to say, on September 18:
The Treasury Board has accepted the principle of evaluating damages, and compensating victims.
How does this square with the statement made in Vancouver last weekend by another cabinet colleague, the government Leader in the Senate, who said:
No consideration has been given by the government to assisting UFFI victims.
Which statement is correct? What is the government's position in getting people out of the mess that you got them into?

subsubtopic: UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speechtext: Madam Speaker, perhaps the President of the Treasury Board will consult with his new cabinet colleague and find out what he did say, and get him to clarify his remarks. It still remains the biggest, most gigantic goof-up by this government or any other government I can remember. The statement made yesterday by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to the effect that testing is being done and results will be revealed, offers no consolation whatever to the many hundreds of thousands of angry and worried people out there who do not know whether to take the insulation out or not.

Madam Speaker,
I will put my supplementary question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Has her department determined what is a safe level of formaldehyde gas in the home? Since her own expert advisory committee on UFFI has reservations about single readings of formaldehyde measurements and is not prepared to recommend any level of formaldehyde exposure as safe, have her officials told the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that the tests being conducted at this time may, at best, be suspect, if not meaningless.

Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having spoken on this subject so many times before in the House of Commons, my first response to an invitation to speak about environmental legislation might simply have been to file my many speeches contained in Hansard and the minutes from the environment committee meetings that I have made over the past seven years.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
During that time the government has continued to fail to add real substance to all environmental legislation. As far back as January 31, 1978, the then member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine said, of my private member's attempts to place environmental legislation before this House of Commons: "First, I would like to congratulate my colleague from Fraser Valley West because, as I have just said, he is a member of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and is greatly concerned with the environment. It could be perhaps said, as all members of this committee are aware, he certainly shows great obstinacy about this problem."
That is why I am standing again today, Mr. Speaker. I should like to continue that obstinacy and my fight for the environmental ethic that is right, that is known to be right, if not by this generation of legislators, certainly the next generation of legislators that will replace us here.
So often the government has brought forward legislation on the environment that is sound in principle, sound in intent; but when you start to look at it, it is full of qualifications, discretion and loopholes; so full, in fact, that the intent is totally negated in the final version of the legislation. This bill is certainly no exception. Having spoken out strongly and in a supportive manner on the environment, the environment has still been given a back seat to the expediency of the energy crisis.
The point is important because of the flexibility the government has established. The response by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is that we need to have good faith-that the government will act and that the government needs discretion. It needs a lot of "may". There are a lot of "ifs"; if this happens, something else will happen. The "mays", the "ifs", the "discretion", are subjective. This subjectiveness is relative and changeable according to the basic intent of the individual minister that holds that portfolio, of the government and of the broad will of the population meeting any immediate crisis as it sees it at that time. Therefore, we need to look at the government's intent.
As I look at the government's intent over the past seven frustrating years, I find that intent is very questionable. While it might initially sound good, the practice has not lived up to any of the billing that has, in fact, been brought forward in the placement of legislation before the House of Commons. For example, one of the main factors we see in this legislation is that the Department of the Environment is not the "need" agency again.
What does this allow for? The Department of the Environment, when the environment is being endangered, is the front line of protest. The Department of the Environment listens sympathetically. It indicates it will press the government; but, of course, it makes the usual qualification that all it can do is press the government because it has no authority.
I am not just imagining these things, Mr. Speaker. These are statements that have been made by ministers. These excuses have already been used time and time again when we are faced with an environmental crisis or threat of any kind.

October 16, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
For example, in 1976 we were talking about Beaufort Sea drilling. We had legislation before us at that time that provided that the minister of the environment "may"-again at his discretion-do certain things. Which minister was the legislation talking about? It was not talking about the then minister of the environment. Even the Minister of the Environment has "mays" and "ifs"; but in this case they are talking about the minister of energy.
In response to that drilling in the Beaufort Sea, the minister of the environment said on March 19, 1976, in the forestry committee, in reply to a question by myself:
Of course, we do not have the authority to oppose in the sense that we can block the decision.
They can only advise. Those are the words of the minister. Under the bill before us the Minister of the Environment will also be able to say, "I do not have the authority". He does not have the authority because this bill did not give the authority to the correct minister, the Minister of the Environment.
Then he was asked, "Who has the authority?" He went on to say:
The permit is issued by Northern Affairs, not by us.
Thus, they are not responsible, and that is the end of the issue. Where do we go from there? We go back to the vested interest instead of in fact a person who has the specific vested interest of the environment and the capacity to act.
The next thing the government tends to do to ensure that one cannot pin down who is really responsible is that it divides the jurisdiction between two, three or four departments. Then each department in turn passes the buck to the next department, and then one gets going in this big circle. I have been through the circle. Anyone who has tried to do anything in the environment has been through the circle. By the time one gets through that circle, one is so tired and worn out, because there has been so much verbiage, that one does not know where to go, so one gives up. The process itself, the sand-in-the-gears process or the passing-the-buck process, in fact destroys the whole capacity of environmental people who are genuinely concerned. It destroys their whole thrust and, in effect, the vested interest rides over in its traditional manner through its access to government. This is again an example of split authority.
When I first came here I complained about these things, but I had no personal experience to show that they were true. Now I have sat through the proceedings of the committee and of the House of Commons. I see what is happening now. It is another piece of legislation where exactly the same thing will happen.
I asked the then minister of the environment, Mr. Mar-chand, whether he thought he should have the authority. I have referred to. Well, he wanted to say, "I think it would be a good idea", but he stopped right there, caught himself and realized that he was not supposed to say that. He went on to say:
You know what kind of jurisdiction we have in Environment, and as the federal government. This jurisdiction is not only split between departments, it is split too between federal and provincial governments.
After we get through three federal departments, down through that cycle, then the next cycle to which we are referred is back to the provincial. Then after that we will be referred back to the municipal. I have been through that cycle too. We sat in White Rock and saw desperate local politicians watching an identified oil slick floating toward the shoreline. I might say that it was a beautiful shoreline. I was a member of the provincial legislature at that time. I was frustrated. I got on the telephone and called the provincial authorities. They said, "No, the oil slick is way out there. It is out in federal jurisdiction; there is nothing we can do." Then it floated to shore. As the tide went out, it was left on the shore and they said, "It is now on the shore; that is municipal jurisdiction". Of course, the municipality had no equipment to fight it. Then what happened? The oil sat there on the shore and in the end the municipality cleaned it up with a bunch of environmental volunteers. The government passed this buck from department to department.
The legislation before us maintains that trend. While it sounds good, it will ensure that there is very little effective result for the people who will be damaged or may be hurt by the actions of the government in co-operation with vested interests. By the way, I respect those vested interests. I respect the need for development. I want the need for development. I do not want to see environmental legislation ever become sand-in-the gears. The government shows an intention, but in fact it is a sand-in-the-gears process.
We need to clarify and make more expedient all environmental law. This bill had potential. When we started with this bill and its expression of intent, it had potential. Again, as expected, that potential has been limited to such an extent as to make it relatively ineffectual. There is another example. We can go from 1976 to 1979. One would think things would have improved three years later. In response to my question, as reported on page 3 of the March 19, 1976, committee meeting, Mr. Marchand said, "I do not have the authority." Actually in that case I think the minister did not want the authority or the responsibility because to be minister of the environment is not an easy job. It is a job where one must make decisions or should have to make decisions. One should be forced by legislation to be able to make decisions and to make decisions stick in the best interests of the environment and of the nation as a whole as it relates to its productivity. We see a shifting of responsibility. I talked about that oil spill and the minister replied on March 20, 1979:
-in the case of this particular oil spill, the Coast Guard and the Ministry of Transport are the lead agencies.
Again it is, "Not me, not me". As we travel on through piece of legislation after piece of legislation, indeed it is unfortunate that these things continue to happen.
I have many specific concerns about this bill. My concerns relate mostly to the fact that this bill should have provided an opportunity to the House of Commons. It should have been
October 16, 1981

one of our last opportunities to entrench environmental principles, values and ethics into the legislation. The reality of the government has shifted. The expediency has shifted slightly toward energy expediency as opposed to environmental reality. But this was a chance. We might not get another chance for a long time. I have been sitting here for a long time awaiting environmental legislation so that we could discuss the issues again and reinforce the issues. At a time when environment is slipping, it needs more emphasis, not less, in the longer term interests of our nation.
This specifically was an opportunity to include some form of automatic or compulsory before the fact environmental impact assessment rather than a specific environmental impact assessment law. We now have some review procedures which are very fuzzy and woolly on the "may" flexibility attitude. This would have been an opportunity to include some "shalls" and an automatic provision for environmental impact assessment.
Now we tend to wait for an accident to occur. The oil arrives on the shore or appears underneath the ocean from a broken pipeline or whatever. The damage is done. Then they say, "We must make an assessment of the damage." They are willing to assess the damage, but they are not really willing to put an assessment on the potential of damage to prevent it before it happens. The whole thrust of legislation starts from the crisis backwards, instead of anticipating and preparing for what might occur through an initial environmental impact assessment. I am not saying that this assessment needs to be long or complicated, but we need that initial assessment. It needs to be a "shall be" assessed, not a "may be" assessed, as this legislation and all other environmental legislation before the House of Commons in fact indicates.
I might make one minor exception. The current minister put some teeth into the Fisheries Act. He tried to remove an awful lot, but he put some in. It is too bad that the government did not have the same initiative and incentive to do so in this piece of legislation.
I am concerned about access to public information-not just access but about freedom of information and public access as well as the publication of that information. It is one thing to table a document in this House and make it public, but it is another to have that document available to the public. As usual, that opportunity is missed in this piece of legislation; it should be there.
This legislation could have firmly established the Department of the Environment as a lead agency of government. I want to come back to the question of what the intent of the government is. Does it intend that the environment should be a major factor in this bill? The intent that the government demonstrates is that the Department of the Environment will not be the lead agency. I think this is the beginning of the end of a phasing out of the Department of the Environment. It will become less and less important. Since the time that Madam Speaker was minister of the environment, virtually nothing has happened. This is the first real response in any form of
Canada Oil and Gas Act
legislation and that is unfortunate, as I see it as a downgrading.
We are almost back to the point of wondering whether the Department of the Environment is necessary at all. When confederation was conceived and the division of authority and responsibility was listed, the environment was not included. At that time people did not think about it but in the 1960s and 1970s it was determined that the environment was important, as it is today and will be tomorrow, and they realized that an ongoing emphasis should be placed on it. Where is that enthusiasm now? At least it established a very professional bureaucracy. We have a competent, complicated bureaucracy in place now and there are competent support groups in the community that bring forward very informed and enlightened information on the environment. The structure is there but the power has not been handed over. The government has not handed over the power because it does not have the intent or the will to establish the department as a lead agency of government. I am concerned about that, Mr. Speaker.
I am also concerned about the control of the environmental studies revolving fund. How is it possible that something with that name could come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources? If that is not obviously an environmental matter, I do not know what is. Why was it not placed under the jurisdiction of the Department of the Environment? That question has not been answered.
I am concerned that the liability provision is too limited and access to benefits is too difficult and improbable. The limitation period is too short. We seem to have the idea that once a problem occurs, we handle it and that is the end of it, when actually environmental problems are often of a long-term nature. That liability should be covered in the legislation and it is not. The period mentioned is too short.
I have mentioned the lack of clarity in regard to jurisdiction and authority and I should like to emphasize it again. We must decide who is responsible and give them full responsibility. If the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is to have input, that is fine; if the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is to have input, that is fine too; but the authority should be given to the environmental agency, the lead agency. This would make for speed and it would clearly help industry and environmentalists to know where the buck stops. They would know that their objective could be reached or rejected, instead of going around in circles.
I am also concerned about the potential irrelevance and the waste of time and money in the allocation of what may turn out to be senseless programs. I am not sure that the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources or the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development can establish the priorities for spending the limited funds available for compensation or for studies. The bureaucracy with the expertise is within the Department of the Environment, not those other two departments. The control should be placed with it so that we can be sure the money will not be wasted on patronage projects. Even worse, in my opinion, is that if the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources allocates the money, it will go

Canada Oil and Gas Act
to buy apologists for what that department wants to do to the Department of the Environment. It will pit environmentalist against environmentalist and leave no money, no authority, no ability with the Department of the Environment to prepare its case. Instead, the other side will be funded. Again, the vested interests receive the advantage and the case for the environment is unheard.
I see that my time is drawing to a close, Mr. Speaker, so I shall conclude.

The environmental ethic grew out of political expediency. The government is now trying to kill the momentum of earlier initiatives on the environment to meet the new political expediency that it now perceives as the energy crisis. The government is wrong, philosophically and morally, in its attempt to have its cake and eat it too.
Although members of the environment community are young, they will not be defeated in this case. Young as they are, they are also intelligent and articulate and will not be deceived by this double standard or the confusions that I have mentioned. While some in this community have been bought as apologists for the vested interest of government and big business, the younger generation has environmental ethics implanted deeply in its value system. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity this afternoon to speak to this particular grouping of motions. It is a very important grouping and refers to the very sensitive environment of northern Canada and offshore areas as well as to the people of northern Canada.
When Bill C-48 was introduced some months ago, I listened to the minister articulate at that time the general thrust of the bill and it sounded nothing short of excellent. It was an effort to begin a process of Canadianization of the petro-chemical industry, starting with oil and gas. There was a sensitivity toward a northern environment and the offshore environment as well as a sensitivity toward people from northern Canada.
Members of this party felt very good about the bill. Then, of course, it went to committee and we had an opportunity to examine it clause by clause and very quickly changed our minds. Upon analysis, the bill showed a real contempt for the people north of 60, an insensitivity to the cultures that exist north of 60 and a complete disregard for and insensitivity toward our fragile northern and offshore ecology.
This does not come as a particular surprise. I guess one has to say that one is a bit ashamed to have some optimism in the early stages of this discussion to think that, in fact, the Liberal Party had changed its tack and was now going to become a party of sensitivity toward the environment and to the people of Canada, especially to the people of northern Canada. As of late, we have seen something in British Columbia which I think demonstrates this even further. That is the decision of the British Columbia government to proceed with burning Hat Creek coal, extremely low grade coal, in an effort to generate electrical power for British Columbia and for export.
At the same time, we understand that concerns about acid rain are increasing, and that there has to be a concern, like never before, regarding the effluent limits, the quality of our effluent entering the atmosphere, in an effort to combat the hazards of acid rain. However, when I inquired of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) how he felt about the Hat Creek proposal, which is a proposal to burn vast amounts of extremely low grade coal with extremely high ash content and with an extremely high content of sulphur and nitrous oxides, his response was, "We have regulations in place now; everything is fine, thank you". That was contrary to the report that the parliamentary task force came out with just a few days ago, indicating that, indeed, things are not all right and that very strict and courageous legislation is required, and required immediately. I, for one, am not optimistic that those difficult and hard decisions will be made, because it would require a government which has a commitment to the environment and a commitment to making difficult decisions; and neither of those commitments adequately describes the Liberal Party of Canada.
I think that the thin edge of the wedge began to show in the committee when the recommendation was that the committee travel throughout northern Canada in an effort to allow northern Canadians to have input into this particular discussion. Now who in their right mind would say that taking discussion of this particular bill, Bill C-48, throughout the part of Canada which will be directly involved would be a bad thing to do, would be too expensive and would be unnecessary? The government decided that. The members of the government on that committee decided that, no, they did not want to seek public input. They did not want to go to the northern parts of Canada and allow people to have an adequate say in this particular piece of legislation.
While I notice that hon. members across the aisle are nodding that that is not the case, sitting through those committee sessions it became very clear that public input of any
October 16, 1981

real substance would not be sought; indeed, the committee members voted in that way, through a stacked vote, to ensure that northern peoples would not have opportunity to dialogue on this important piece of legislation.
It begs the question: Why is the government afraid of public input on Bill C-48? I suspect that in the hearts of government members, they know that what they are attempting to do with Bill C-48 is inappropriate as we enter the 1980s. When I say "inappropriate as we enter the 1980s", I refer to a sensitivity which is growing across the country, particularly with young people. There is a growing understanding of our complex ecological environment, and understanding of the intricate and comprehensive ecological webs that make Canada possible, and a growing understanding of the fragile and unique environment north of 60. Here is a part of Canada which still bears the imprints of groups of people who lived in that environment decades ago. Machinery which was brought into the area 40 or 50 years ago still leaves its imprint across those tundra wastes. Ask the native people of northern Canada what has happened to the caribou herds, to the movements of the sealing populations, and to the whale hunt. One could go on and on but the response will always be the same. They are changing, and changing not for the improvement of life north of 60, but changing for the betterment of life south of 60.
The intent of Bill C-48 is to accelerate exploration for oil and gas in the lands that we call Canada lands, including the Yukon, Northwest Territories and offshore. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) says that it is a step to Canadianize the oil and gas industry. What we are saying in these particular amendments we are debating at the moment is that, regardless whether these are foreign companies operating in the sensitive environmental areas or whether they are Canadian owned and controlled companies, the problems are still the same.
This bill lacks sensitivity to that very crucial and critical environment, both in human and in natural terms. We are going to be seeing the decimation of a culture that we have come to describe as the Inuit culture. We are going to see the disappearance of the Metis culture of northern Canada, and we are certainly going to see the ecological balances of northern Canada upset dramatically if Bill C-48 proceeds as it is presently proposed.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman), who spoke previously, indicated that real environmental impact assessments are not called for in this legislation. In any textbook, in any symposium, or in any discussion around a sensitive environment, the bottom line that one would always expect is the need for a sophisticated system of environmental impact statements; but Bill C-48 virtually totally ignores that. It is after the fact, which again portrays and demonstrates very clearly this government's lack of interest in preserving that fragile ecological balance in northern Canada and offshore.
Exploration, at what cost? I become very frightened when I look at bills such as Bill C-48 and see all of the powers that are vested in ministers' discretion. I become very concerned when I see the Minister of the Environment, the Minister of Fisheries
Canada Oil and Gas Act
and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) being given the power to make decisions on the state of affairs on the Canada lands. This is no reflection necessarily on the existing ministers. They are all fine and very capable individuals. They are not here, of course. However, what about future ministers? What about people who will be filling those positions in years to come? Do we have confidence in those people? We do not even know who they are; yet Bill C-48 is asking us to have open-ended confidence in the Liberal government, in the Liberal cabinet, in their ability to make decent, sensible, sensitive decisions regarding, primarily, the lands north of 60.

There is no formal protective status in Bill C-48 for these 150 special world sites. I am sure I speak for everyone in this House when I say that we are concerned about the wildlife of northern Canada. We recognize that we are viewed the world over as having special concerns about our wildlife in the north.
While we have taken some small steps over the last number of years to preserve the wildlife of Canada, only six federal wildlife biologists are given the responsibility for that vast expanse of northern space. How on earth could six wildlife biologists even begin to patrol and manage that particular area adequately? They would have difficulty doing that on Prince Edward Island, let alone on Canada lands north of 60.
What about the claims of the native people in the lands north of 60? Surely before Bill C-48 proceeds any further, this is a sensitivity that we can no longer ignore. Here are peoples whose lives, let alone cultures, are in serious jeopardy. Here are people who live in one of the most fragile environments in the world, into which we are now rushing pell mell to explore for oil and gas, who have no say in the proceedings, no say about what happens to their own land and whose land claims issues are totally ignored. Good grief, how could any group of people in a House of Commons responsible for that major and crucial part of Canada be so insensitive?

My constituency is in northern Ontario. Ontario is a large province, but my area, which is relatively small, has been negotiating with our pulp and paper companies. After a period of 50 or 60 years, we have now reached the point where we are running out of trees in our area. This is because the province of Ontario has been manipulating. The smaller the jurisdiction, the easier it is to manipulate.
I would have been much happier if those resources had been in the hands of the federal government, particularly at this stage when the federal government is really concerned about global corporations, multinational oil companies and the effect they are having on our country.
Regarding the offshore resources of the north, or Newfoundland, if control of these resources is in the hands of a province, the territories or the Dene people, they can be easily manipulated. I have talked to the Dene people and I have talked to people in Newfoundland about these things, and they have said they are not easily manipulated. But the history of the native people in this country has shown that they have been constantly manipulated. It is easier to manipulate a small jurisdiction.
I support the government in this area. The most fair and sensible thing to do to maintain these resources intact is to have a sharing arrangement like the one offered to the province of Newfoundland and the one apparently offered to the province of Nova Scotia concerning their offshore resources. Therefore, these resources will not be manipulated as easily as they could be in smaller jurisdictions.
The history concerning the manipulation of resources is the same all over-in Australia, in the United States and so on. Wherever resources were in the hands of a small area, they were manipulated. I suggest that we go for a sharing arrangement.

Mr. Speaker, as always I am very pleased to rise in my place and speak in this House during what will surely be an historic session. We are dealing today with the report stage of Bill C-48. I want to say, first of all, that I attended literally all of the committee hearings on this bill and have made a number of recommendations, as did other members of the Progressive Conservative Party, recommendations which are all on record. We spent some eight months on this bill in committee and heard from representatives from industry, from the banking society, from environmental groups, from the native people, from territorial governments and other organizations.
Effectively the government has told us that all the amendments which are to be made to this bill have been made in committee. At the report stage when speaking in this House we are speaking more for the record, indeed, waxing long and loud on a topic that is dear to most of our hearts; that is, environmental management in Canada.
I am not going to speak so much about the detail of the amendments before us as I am going to speak on the over-all umbrella of environmental management and environmental awareness in Canada. The federal government is today moving in a somewhat different direction on environmental management in Canada, and I think it is a direction that has to be examined carefully by Canadians and the Canadian government.
The decade of the 1970s saw a great awareness of environmental issues. In particular, the first half of the 1970s was an era or a time in Canadian history when environmental concerns, awareness and action was pervasive across the land, literally starting with the formation of the first department of the environment in the province of Alberta, formed by the Social Credit government in Alberta in the spring of 1971. Since that time literally every government in Canada at the provincial and national levels has formed a department of the environment.
In addition, the Canadian Council on Resources, whose first chairman was the hon. Mr. Levesque, changed its name. Environmental aspects were incorporated into that council, which became the Canadian Council on Resources and Environment Ministers. The environment took on a very prominent role in the considerations and discussions of ministers across this nation. A new realization of the relationship between development and preservation and development and Environmental management of those resources evolved in the 1970s.
At the beginning of the 1980s we are now embarking on a new direction. We are now saying we must develop at all costs. Particularly in one area of resource management, the energy
Canada Oil and Gas Act
industry, we are now saying that the need to sustain energy at present society consumption levels must take preference over environmental management, environment concerns and environmental direction. That is why I say this whole area of movement into a new era of environmental awareness and action must be examined carefully.
I remember so well the 1972 Stockholm conference on the human environment as I was a Canadian delegate. Well I remember a resolution by the United States delegation which said unequivocally that a nation must be responsible for its pollutants as they migrate across international boundaries. I remember how we all supported that resolution of the United States of America. I am not overly excited with some of the congressional statements of today, that perhaps the migration of pollutants across international boundaries is not so important any more and must take a back seat to other considerations. This is rationalization in the 1980s regarding the maintenance of a way of life that was developed in an inefficient way.
It is this attitude that I see also creeping in in Canada, not only at the federal level but, indeed, at the provincial level. Now that we have gone through that decade of environmental awareness, we must find a different direction, and to a large degree we are moving forth step in step with the United States, not only in monetary and economic policies but in environmental policies.
Recently this government signed an energy agreement with Alberta. Three precedents were established within that agreement as far as I am concerned. It was a reasonable national agreement and a reasonable agreement for the province of Alberta. What were those three precedents? The first is an indication of a new era of federal-provincial relations which says that to conclude an agreement the federal government will negotiate in a serious manner with one province and then impose that agreement, one by one, on each of the other provinces in Canada.
I believe the federal government has questioned the value of first ministers' conferences. During the tenure of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in this House, his government has had more first ministers' conferences than any other government in history. I believe the government has decided that first minister's conferences accomplish very little and a new system must be found, and that is to reach an agreement with a province without meeting all of the first ministers and then imposing that agreement on the other provincial governments. This is exactly what is happening with the energy agreement.
I believe the government feels that by placing ten Premiers around the table in front of television cameras, Canadians see these ten Premiers and the Prime Minister sitting together as equals and the stature of the Prime Minister is thus depreciated in the context of confederation. I believe we are seeing a new era in federal-provincial relations, evidenced by the agreement between Alberta and the federal government.

Canada Oil and Gas Act
The second and equally important precedent is that provinces can now cut flowing resources and interrupt them with impunity. I repeat, provinces can now cut flowing resources with impunity to accomplish their own objective. It does not matter whether they are resources owned by the provinces or developed and owned by the private sector. Alberta did it with oil. What province will be next? Will Newfoundland cut its electrical production by 10 per cent, 20 per cent or 30 per cent to restructure their agreement with the province of Quebec? The precedent is there. Alberta indicated that if there was an emergency in Canada with regard to the supply of oil they would restore production, therefore negating the use of the emergency powers. I found it very hard for the federal government to act against Alberta cutting this resource when Section 57 in the constitutional resolution said unequivocally that the provinces were the sole governments that could legislate in the area of conservation, production and distribution of their resources.
The third precedent I see is that there is not one clause in the agreement with Alberta about environmental concerns, no allocation of a single dollar, either federally or provincially, for environmental management as a result of the development and exploitation of energy resources in Canada. This five year agreement envisions a massive tertiary recovery process which has tremendous environmental consequences. It envisions heavy oil plants which could result in enormous environmental consequences. It envisions additional oil sands plants and exploration and development of new sour gas finds in Canada.
I received a phone call recently from people in Pincher Creek who suffered from sour gas and hydrogen sulphide pollution for years, unknown elements, indicating to me that there is a new direction in relationship to the control of sour gas in southern Alberta. Hydrogen sulphide, sulphur dioxide and acid rain emanating from this type of development is increasing in southern Alberta.
I want to come back to Bill C-48. There is a new environmental direction prevalent throughout this bill. If I were to paraphrase a metaphor effectively depicting the role of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) in this bill, I would perhaps say that he is going to be as effective as a toad among an army of ground hogs all intent on drilling holes in the ground. The Minister of the Environment will not be very effective in relation to Bill C-48.
That is right.

There are two environmental aspects to this bill. First, the environmental regulatory function is entirely under the thumb of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) through the resource management branch of Energy, Mines and Resources. Second, there is the study, investigative, and research function. To perform this function you need money. Within this bill there is a structure for two funds. One fund is under the direction and administration of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The second fund is under the administration of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro). Somehow
the Minister of the Environment has to direct the flow of this money under the direction of the other two ministers. The Department of the Environment provides input into massive development of oil and gas on Canada lands through an interdepartmental forum known as the resource management environmental committee. This committee is the main interdepartmental forum through which formal communication can take place on environmental issues relating to offshore oil and gas activities. It provides a co-ordinated approach to environmental assessment and research programs for offshore operations under the administration of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Let me enlighten the House as to who is represented on this committee. The first representative is the resource management branch of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. The second representative is the office of environmental affairs in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. The third is the fisheries management branch within the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. The fourth representative is the ocean science and survey section under the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. The fifth is the atmospheric environmental service under the Department of the Environment. The sixth is the environmental conservation service under the Department of the Environment, and the seventh is the environmental protection service under the Department of the Environment. Three representatives on this committee are from the Department of the Environment, two from Energy, Mines and Resources and two from Fisheries and Oceans.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is not even represented on this committee. I find that strange. More important, it is not the Department of the Environment and its minister, not even the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and its minister, which have over-all control and funding of investigations as a result of this committee, but rather the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and its minister. This is not even in the control and regulatory function, who is totally within EM&R. It is in the study function, investigative function and research function.
One would think if foremost in the minds of these civil servants were environmental matters or fisheries that that committee would be under the auspices of the Department of the Environment or the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, not the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. Obviously that is subordinate to the new philosophy of development at any cost.
I know the internal jockeying, persuasiveness and arm-twisting that goes on in such committees. As the former minister of the environment in Alberta, I have done a lot of public hearings and conducted studies. I know how often the minister must act as the adjudicator, take the initiative and push the committee in a certain direction which is relevant to the requirements of the day. It will be the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who will be controlling the direction of
October 16, 1981

this study committee. The least we can do is transfer the responsibility of this committee to where it belongs.
Where is the Minister of the Environment in all of this? What is his role in Bill C-48? One can almost say he is the water boy for the energy football team which is being quarterbacked by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and coached by the Prime Minister. A great football team, a great football game! The projected energy reserves on land in Canada are six billion barrels of oil and 85 trillion cubic feet of gas, which is equivalent to 20 billion barrels of oil. On the west coast offshore, we have mainly gas reserves of supposedly seven trillion cubic feet which is equivalent to two billion barrels of oil.
In total offshore resources we have approximately 15 to 20 billion barrels of oil and 250 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, equivalent to some 60 billion barrels. Apart from the heavy oil in the oil sands, one just has to look at these figures to see the tremendous amount of development activity that will occur in Canada in offshore the next 25 to 50 years.
This is a big ball game. The equivalent of 60 billion barrels of energy puts us in the big league. Because the game is so vast, the Minister of the Environment and the national government had better play a more significant role in the whole area of development than that identified in Bill C-48.

I might indicate that, after some discussion with the Chair, one member from the New Democratic Party would like to get away this afternoon. Since 1 see no member to my right, perhaps members might convenience the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle). If it is agreeable, I will recognize him now and then proceed to the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro).
That is quite satisfactory to me, Mr. Speaker. There may be others who also have to get away. I give my concurrence.
We will proceed accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, I feel happy and privileged to speak to Bill C-48 in the area that concerns the environmental sections, Motions Nos. 4, 34, 51, 52, 53, 55, 56 and 57, under discussion at this time.
Bill C-48 will without a doubt have a great influence on the future not only of our country but of the whole planet. It will make a very significant mark upon the environment of a great part of this planet. When one faces a problem of this magnitude with effects that could go down not just through our generation but through many generations that will follow, 1 and many others believe with me that we are facing a serious moral issue of a magnitude that we have very little experience in handling. Basically we are dealing with a moral issue that does not just affect me and those around me at this moment; it will affect the lives of literally millions of people who are yet unborn, yet unthought of, in various ways.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
First, when we begin to deal with something that is finite, that has a limit-and the kinds of energies we are looking at now are something that will be used up or taken away-that is one big question. The other moral question is: In finding or taking away this source of finite quality, what is the morality in the sense of breaking down the environmental structure of the planet? That is the question we face.
When we were young, morality was something that could be handled quite easily. If as a little kid I broke the neighbour's window, my family would send me over to say I was sorry and we would have to make some kind of restitution. Morality was simple, we could handle it. However, what happens when you break a structure that will have an influence for 20, 30, 40 or how many centuries are left on the planet? That is basically what this kind of bill is doing.
In the recent past, and I am talking of the past 100 years, our forefathers-my father, my grandfather and so on-felt there was no great problem in using up all the resources they could see. Many times I spoke to my father, now dead, asking why his generation felt it was perfectly morally legitimate to take over pieces of land from Winnipeg to the Rocky Mountains and use the resources in one generation without leaving any kind of reserve for the future, using them up many times in such a way that they literally destroyed the environment within two decades.
If people can remember the thirties in Saskatchewan, and some in this House certainly can, then they would remember the way the prairie was dug up, broken down, blown away and destroyed, never to be returned to the kind of land it was. We are again dealing with a situation of that kind. What is the morality of now doing that to the planet? I in no way claim I have the right answer to a question of that kind, but I do know, in looking at other situations and seeing other places, that the model of development in the field of energy at this time is one that has already broken down great sections of the planet.
A couple of days ago I was in Chicago and south of Chicago, down toward Notre Dame, Indiana. When you drive from Chicago to Notre Dame you go through the steel area of Gary and so on. Right there, as a cold, hard fact, we have a kind of an abomination, a desolation where the industrial model that was developed in the last 100 years has literally destroyed and broken down part of the planet. The air is gone; the water is gone; the land is gone. The people there live in a rusting, broken desert. That space on the planet 100 years ago was a fruitful, green garden. We are asking those kinds of questions.
What I would like to do in my speech today, Mr. Speaker, is to introduce into Hansard what I would call a scriptural phrase-a group of "voices crying in the wilderness". In this discussion I should like to introduce the thoughts of some people whom I consider in the present day, in the moral situation created by this bill, to be voices crying in the wilderness. I refer to church groups.

When Bill C-48 was announced and its effects were beginning to be known, on March 18 of this year two Anglican and three Roman Catholic bishops issued a statement in relation to the morality of this bill. They were the Right Rev. Jack Sperry, Anglican Bishop of the Arctic; the Right Rev. R. Ferris, Anglican Bishop of the Yukon; the Most Rev. Hubert O'Connor, Roman Catholic Bishop of the Yukon; the Most Rev. Paul Piche, Roman Catholic Bishop of Mackenzie-Fort Smith; and the Most Rev. Omer Robidoux, Roman Catholic Bishop of Churchill-Hudson's Bay. Their statement is as follows:
As leaders of the northern churches, we appreciate the work of the northern political leaders during their two-day conference at Yellowknife, March 18 and 19, 1981, and we support their firm opposition to Bill C-48.
Bill C-48 denies the aboriginal rights of the native people, as well as the present mandate of the northern institution of government. It is a negation of the present and future rights of all the residents of the Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory.
We therefore join the Yukon and Northwest Territories government, Committee for Original People's Entitlement, Dene nation, Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, Council of Yukon Indians, and Northwest Territories Metis Association in urging the Government of Canada to completely withdraw Bill C-48.
Furthermore, we call on the Government of Canada to effectively involve northern native and political leaders in the drafting of any new oil and gas legislation so as to ensure that the people of the north will truly benefit from the future development of resources.
This statement was issued by the five northern bishops on March 18 and 19,1981.
On March 25, 1981, the Most Rev. Remi J. De Roo, Chairman of the Episcopal Commission for Social Affairs of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, wrote a personal letter and a telex to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in which the same concerns were brought forth in regard to this present bill. He wrote as follows;
In effect, this proposed legislation would further entrench the people of the north in a situation of colonialism in Canada. It not only threatens to violate the aboriginal rights of the native peoples but it also threatens to deny all the peoples of the north some of the basic democratic rights and freedoms which we have come to know and expect in other regions of Canada.
The telex also indicated the great fear of danger to the environment in this bill's proposals.
On June 9, 1981, as all hon. members are aware, the Canadian Conference of Bishops wrote a personal letter to each member of the House of Commons. They outlined their basic fears and lack of true preparation and consultation in relation to the same bill. Every Member of Parliament received that letter.
On June 12, 1981, the Most Rev. Joseph MacNeil, Archbishop of Edmonton, who is the president of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, prepared a statement on why the bishops' conference opposed Bill C-48 on two grounds: first, the environmental impact; second, on the question of the involvement of the native and local peoples, or their noninvolvement, I should say, in the preparation of the bill.
On June 17, 1981, the Minister for Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) replied to the letter of Bishop Remi De Roo that was sent to all members of the
House of Commons. They indicated that the bishops did not know what they were talking about. I think it would be possible for the bishops to say the ministers might not know what they were talking about.
Hear, hear!

The letter reads as follows:
From the specific comments you make on the bill, we believe that you have been seriously misinformed as to its content and implications.
It is an opinion, I agree. Then they went on to say:
As Canadian citizens we are saddened that, before you took a stand, no effort was made to reach us in order to give us an opportunity to at least expose our point of view and go with you through the proposed legislation. We respectfully submit that, had you done so, you might have reached very different conclusions as to the intent and the nature of the legislation. In fact, you might very well have become convinced, as we are, that Bill C-48 represents a major improvement over the previous situation for all Canadians, including the aboriginal peoples whose interests the government as well as yourself have very much at heart.
Following that reply, a meeting was arranged between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and a representative of the Canadian Bishops Conference, Bishop Sherlock of London. The bishops again set forth the reason why the churches had this grave concern about the moral issues that were involved in the bill and which were not being properly handled.
Bishop Sherlock, in a report following that meeting, said that the meeting was amicable but that he did not think anyone was convinced. I suspect that was exactly the situation.
Following that, on October 14, the day upon which the House resumed, Bishop Remi J. De Roo sent a final letter asking the Government of Canada to rethink the comments in its former letter in respect of Bill C-48. He pointed out the reasons why Canadian bishops feel that we are dealing with a serious moral question.
That is the state of the question and how Canadian churches have attempted to influence what is going on. However, I feel that they are literally voices crying in the wilderness. The difficulty at this time is for us to grasp the seriousness of the total problem which Bill C-48 envisages. It is simply just that; it is difficult.
How do people, myself and yourselves, make a serious moral judgment about a matter which is so huge? I would say that we should make it carefully. We should look at the serious lack of judgment in relation to the environment, to native rights and so forth, in the development of the west, from where I come. In that instance they were not considered. What was the final effect? What happened there? What happened to the rights of native peoples? What happened to the land, the soil, the water and so forth? We have a bit of history to call upon.
No one can predict exactly what will happen in the future. All I can say is that my recent experiences in Canada, North America and other countries indicate that the planet is breaking down at a rate which I am sure no one 20 years ago would have ever expected. The pollution of the oceans, the pollution

of the air, the destruction of land and the disappearance of trees could not have been foreseen just a few years ago. When I was in high school I do not think I ever heard the word pollution. Now it is a word that little children know about. This is something which has happened in our life time. It has been a sort of movement without knowledge into the environment. Pollution and the changing of natural connections or, as someone said a little earlier, national networks of the environment are far bigger problems to face than even atomic bombs. We know the effect of atomic bombs, but we do not know the effect of these encroachments into the environment.
I am happy for this opportunity to present a few words and thoughts. I hope they will have some influence upon the final decision in regard to this bill.

Mr. Speaker, the amendments we are considering this afternoon are concerned with environmental hazard. They are attempting to define a spill, to report a spill, the liability of the person responsible for a spill, the setting up of a compensation fund for recompensing injured parties, the responsibility for long-range damaging effects of spills and inquiries into spills. These are all centred around the notion of environmental hazard. We are discussing a physical contaminant and the threat it poses to the plant and animal ecology of a vast region and to the society of that region.
The hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) related some of the effects of the proposals before us on society. All these matters relate to amendments in this area. Most of them are amendments to amendments to another bill.
In this connection and as an aside, I should like to complain about the absence in the bill as presented to us of the sections of the original act which we are intending to amend in that absence. Hon. members are required to reach for the relevant volumes of the Revised Statutes of Canada in order to see how the original text read. Having done so, they are required to determine whether in fact it is being changed in a desirable way and to speculate on why the changes are being made and whether they are acceptable. I hope the draftsmen who prepare bills in the future will bear this in mind and be of assistance to us in readopting a long-established practice, which is perhaps even a convention of the House, that the old and new legislation should be printed on opposing pages for easy cross-reference by those of us in the House who are dealing with these measures.
I should now like to return to the proposed amendments, the spills and the responsibility therefor. They are all related to the environment. The spills under consideration and the associated liability would be taking place in the so-called Canada lands, or in offshore waters which are carefully defined. Although I admit spills can occur on land and cause damage, my concerns here are only with marine disasters.
Clause 76 refers to exploration and drilling for, and the production, conservation, processing and transportation of, oil and gas in the Canada lands. My concern is basically with the

maritime disasters which can occur. I will confine my remarks to this maritime aspect of the Canada lands.
My concern in this connection is paramount because the area in which these disasters could occur is not only great but vast. I cannot help wondering whether the ministers concerned have any real appreciation of how great and vast the newly-defined maritime area is. Of course, this is defined in Clause 2 of the bill which was being discussed on Wednesday. Also it is defined, in so far as the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act is concerned, in Clause 76 in almost the same terms. To the extent that those terms may differ from those in Clause 2, I think we may have cause to wonder as to the reason for those differences; but I will just leave that aside for the moment.
What really concerns me Mr. Speaker, is whether the minister, members of this House and the Canadian public have any clear notion of the extent of jurisdiction being assumed for environmental protection purposes in offshore waters by this bill in the glib phrase "Canada lands" or, perhaps more properly, "Canada lands and Canada seas". Over what sort of area does the bill extend Canada's jurisdiction for environmental concerns? That is my first question.
My second question is whether Canada is in any position to assume that extended responsibility. I speak about extended jurisdiction over water only, or over water, ice and archipelago. I think we can all envisage the land mass north of 60, but perhaps the seaward extension, according to this definition, is much greater than any of us realize.
We are talking of the 200-mile limit and then to the edge of the continental shelf, whichever is greater. First of all-and I think this needs to be underlined-the 200-mile limit would extend Canada's jurisdiction for environmental protection over an extra 1,300,000 square miles, on the east coast, the west coast and in the Arctic. In that I include the archipelago in the Arctic. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, 1,300,000 square miles. This is slightly greater than the land surface of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan combined. Are we ready for that responsibility, at sea and from the air, in terms of clean-up? When the jurisdiction of the Canadian government was extended to the 200-mile limit by order in council for fisheries purposes, I asked whether we were prepared to assume that responsibility.
If we go out to the continental margin, we add another 285,000 square miles to that 1,300,000 square miles, most of which goes beyond the 200-mile limit found off the east coast-Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and the mouth of the St. Lawrence. Therefore, we are required to add another Alberta to the Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan surface area that we have to bear in mind is the new jurisdiction over which Canada will assume its responsibility in environmental terms.
What does that mean in relation to the present known land and lake surface of Canada as we can more or less grasp it in our minds? It is almost 40 per cent more than the land mass

that we can see from the edge of the Arctic coastline down to the sixtieth parallel and on down to the forty-ninth parallel. That is a tremendous area of jurisdiction.
I wonder if hon. members are aware that what is involved in this extension of jurisdiction is, in reality, an extension for economic purposes to the limits permitted under the Law of the Sea Convention to create, in effect, Canada's exclusive economic zone, or the EEZ, foreseen in that convention.
By sheer coincidence, the definitions in Clauses 2 and 76 of the bill use the wording that appears in Article 76 of the Law of the Sea Convention. What seems to be happening now happened once before. Canada is proceeding unilaterally to assume jurisdiction over an exclusive economic zone of 200 miles, as well as over an additional area to the edge of the continental margin, if that is farther offshore.
We seem to be proceeding unilaterally, as we did in the case of fisheries in assuming jurisdiction over the 200-mile fishing zone. That action, which was effected by order in council, was preceded by a number of bilateral treaties securing recognition-buying recognition, if you will-from countries which had historic rights in that area. This time the claim is being made by legislative action and there is no evidence that the government has concluded any bilateral agreements with neighbours or others, or that counter-claims against our pretensions will not arise in future.
I am not taking serious issue with the government on these grounds for behaving in this way, but I think we should be aware of what is going on. I suspect that one reason for this action is the fear that the Law of the Sea Convention may be in jeopardy because of the attitude of the United States and its explicit objections to the Law of the Sea Convention which were revealed in Geneva during the summer.
Is this, then, I ask myself, a pre-emptive strike on staking claims out to sea? I think it might be. Be that as it may, I have to ask myself whether Canada is in a position, with its maritime surveillance forces-surface and air-and its cleanup forces, to tend this extra real estate which is 40 per cent more than we now "own" and which we seem only indifferently able to regulate for environmental purposes as it is. Are we biting off more than we can chew, let alone digest? That is one of the questions which inevitably strikes me when 1 consider the extent of the claims in this bill.
My suspicions about this legislation were aroused following the intervention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) on Wednesday last when he claimed that the matter was not one of ownership but of how proceeds resulting from the exploitation of the resources found in that land and sea area are to be shared. There is no evidence in this bill of sharing.
I would believe him if he would agree to an amendment which would permit the introduction, particularly in the offshore areas-not the land and lake areas-of some notion of the Queen in right of the provinces as well as the Queen in right of Canada, if only as an and/or proposition, so that the Queen in right of the provinces would know that there could be
an element of sharing in the resources that are available. As matters now stand, it is only the Queen in right of Canada who will have a role in the proceeds of Canada lands and federal jurisdiction in the exploitation of offshore resources.
Canada lands and federal jurisdiction are readily understandable in terms of terra firma. Surely we can all understand that. We are talking now of north of 60. When it comes to the offshore areas, that meaning is fraught with federal-provincial conflict unless some acknowledgement is made in the matter of the claims which the Queen in right of the provinces might have.
A simple acknowledgement of this would do much to dampen current fears of a sea grab, if I may use an expression parallel to the land grab notion with which we are all familiar. Therefore, I have misgivings about the text before us on two grounds: one, I fear that Canada is in no real position to assume the full measure of the environmental commitments it is proposing to assume in this bill; two, I fear that by ignoring the Queen in right of the provinces, the claims, in fact, are a federal claim to ownership for all time without impediment or fetter, thereby storing up for Canada further grounds for federal-provincial conflict, which we just do not need these days.
There is another aspect which worries me. Others before me, and the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko), in particular, spoke about the questionable or light role-or probably the absence of it-that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) would have to play as minister under the terms of Bill C-48. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) are the only ministers mentioned who would have any powers. Yet the legislation acknowledges the environmental impact of oil and gas development. Why is the Department of the Environment excluded?
One other department has been excluded, and I draw this to the attention of the minister sitting in the House. The Department of Transport is excluded from playing any role under this bill. Yet his department, under its jurisdiction, has in existence a maritime pollution claims fund, which is a vehicle which could easily be adapted to this particular bill for claims for damage in environmental terms under this bill. Why has his department been completely set aside? Therefore, I add a third concern. I mentioned the one about the federal-provincial conflict. I have also mentioned the absence of the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin).
From the bill, not from the House.
I do feel that this bill has shortcomings. It ought to go back to the drawing board and be brought forward with a more mature package of proposals for the consideration of this House.

As I have said before in this House, in my opinion Bill C-48 is the greatest land grab, the greatest grab of resources by a Liberal government in the whole history of Canada. We have debated Bill C-48, a copy of which I have here, since Christmas of last year, if I remember rightly. Some changes have been made, mainly of a technical nature. I guess the bill has been improved somewhat. However, if one looked through it now, one would find that it is very much of a cut and paste job. I hope that the government will take this bill back and maybe redraft it. Even if it will not make any changes in the underlying philosophy, it should at least tidy up the drafting and come back with a bill which has not been chopped up and switched around with small additions here and there, but one which makes sense right from the start. In my opinion, it will be pretty difficult for the courts to interpret some of what we have heard.
It is said that maybe some minor improvements have been made in the technicalities of the bill; but the concepts contained in Bill C-48 remain identical to those of the bill when it was first presented. The concept remains that Ottawa should have complete control over all the so-called Canada lands whether, in fact, they really belong to the provinces or to the territories. The industry should be highly regulated. There should be a good deal of ministerial discretion. You do not know what the rules and regulations are in advance, but you have to come to Ottawa and you make your own deal with the minister. What is ministerial discretion? The minister can tell you how you can look for oil, how you can drill for it, to whom you can sell it and how you can transport it, along with everything else, but we do not know the rules in advance. It is a highly regulated and controlled industry. It is one in which there will be practically no room for the little guys, especially the northerners, the people without much capital. They would like to get into the oil and gas business. They would like to get into the land plays, but because of the regulated nature of the industry, the way it is seen from Ottawa, the little guys, the northerners, will be kicked right out of the northern oil patch.
But worst of all for the north and for the northerners, Liberal policy comes through quite clear in this bill, namely, that the resources of the north will in perpetuity, for ever and ever, belong to the federal government in Ottawa. This is something to which we cannot subscribe. In no way would the gentlemen over there want another Alberta on their hands or another Saskatchewan. speechtext: No way.

The government has not actually done anything about it.
Perhaps I might digress for a moment or two, Mr. Speaker. You gave that privilege to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. With respect to Motion No. 2 there is a preamble which hon. members on the other side want to put in front of the bill. I do not like preambles to legislation. 1 think the law books should contain law and not motherhood statements in front of a particular statute. Anyway, if that is what hon. members on the other side want to do, let us examine what they want to say. Before the law they want a whereas clause. Part of the whereas clause will read "Recognizing that in particular the inhabitants of areas directly affected by energy activities would play a growing role in that development."
That is all the government has done. All the arguments, all the letters and all the great speeches that have been made in this House-that is as far as the government can go. I would submit they are no more than empty platitudes. What we need is something real. I have been playing with words and I have come up with something that we might put in place of the above whereas clause. It is something with some teeth in it and something that means something. Instead of the government's preamble, we suggest the following or something like it:
And whereas it is acknowledged that Her Majesty in right of Canada presently holds the lands and resources of the Northwest Territories and Yukon in trust for the inhabitants thereof and hereby agrees to enter into agreements with the governments of the respective territories to share the public revenues derived from the production of hydrocarbons therefrom.
In our clause you have the acknowledgement that the lands and the resources of the north should be held not in perpetuity by the Ottawa government, but held in trust and should be managed as well as any good trustee would manage those resources for the people who live there. They should be managed as well as are the land and resources in the southern provinces of Canada.
In addition, what that would do would be to open up the question of revenue sharing. Many submissions were made on this subject to the committee when it looked into this matter. I think in general members on all sides of this House-not the government members, the frontbenchers, or government departments, but the backbenchers on that side and the members on this side-believe that agreements should be entered into whereby the very large amounts of public revenue to be generated as a result of Bill C-48 should be shared with northerners and used to help the people who live in those areas through the provision of public services. As a matter of right, people should have access to some of that revenue.
Within the bill we have before us, we see that only lip service has been paid to the wishes and the requirements of northerners. What is being said is, "We are not going to give you any real control over these matters, but we will come to you and ask you for your advice. We will set up a little advisory board here and a little advisory committee there and you can have your say, you can collect $25 or $100 a day honorarium and we will listen to you." But we know what happens. There are thousands of these committees already all over the north. Some bureaucrat from Terasse de la Chaudiere arrives, listens to the people, writes notes and minutes and takes them back to Ottawa. Nobody sees what happens to them. I suppose a report is written and it is submitted to the lowest level of bureaucracy in Hull. Then this report has to go step by step by step up to the assistant deputy minister and, the deputy minister, but at any one of these stages, that report can be filed or put into the wastepaper basket. It never sees the light of day. That is the nature of consultation which this government has always practised with the people of the north. Very often this government does not even do that because decisions have already been made in advance. They send someone up north to try and justify the decisions that have already been taken.
We have seen this with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Department of the Environment and everything else. We do not need people to come up north and say "Yes, we will listen to your views, take them back to Ottawa, put them in the mill and see what comes out the other end." What is needed is delegation of authority to the people who live there.
Let us take the environment as a case in point. Presumably we are supposed to be talking about an environmental amendment. People do not want to be consulted about the seals, the seagulls, the rabbits and everything else in the north and then have someone return to Ottawa and make up rules and recommendations, hopefully taking their advice into account. What they want is the authority to make their own rules. We are not talking about the offshore areas because presumably the federal government has some constitutional right to be in that area. But the federal government does not have to have it in the land areas of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. If the area were a province, that responsibility would lie with the province. In fact under the Northwest Territories Act and under the Yukon Act, that responsibility has in a way been given, but then it has been taken back by the federal government. Right now in the Northwest Territories there is an act of the local legislature, called the Environmental Protection Ordinance. But it is not in force because, as I said before, the government there has no money and no source of revenue. The government

Most of us realize that as well as having facts to argue on a particular case, we have to deal with the mythology that for some reason or other, tends to permeate any debate at any level. This debate on Bill C-48 is no exception. In fact, from what I have heard in the House in the last few days and in committee in the last few months there is probably more mythology involved in this debate than in almost any other debate, other than perhaps the debate on the Constitution.
In the short time allotted to me today, I would like to look at some of the myths that have developed and are promoted by their proponents as being the hard truths of the argument. I would like to start with one of the myths that was forcefully and colourfully projected into this debate today by the preceding speaker. That myth is that the central or national government is perpetrating through Bill C-48 one of the greatest or most momentous land grabs in the history of the Canadian people.
The offshore and the north are vested and always have been vested in Her Majesty in right of Canada. I do not think there is anyone in this House who can dispute the accuracy and legitimacy of that statement. It is vested in Her Majesty in right of Canada because all the federal states of this world have vested the rights of the offshore, and, presumably, if they have an Arctic, in the national government in one way or another.
I would defy any member opposite to point out a federation in this world that has done otherwise. Assuming that the federation has an offshore and a north, despite the fact that the waters and domains have historically been vested in the central government, it has not prevented its regional or provin-

Canada Oil and Gas Act
cial governments from making a jurisdictional grab of their own.
