subsubtopic: AVAILABILITY OF INCREASING GRANTS IN LIEU OF PROPERTY TAXES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of increasing the grants made to municipalities in lieu of property taxes for the use of property by Crown corporations and agencies so that these grants equal the sums paid by private organizations.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of presenting what I believe to be a case that should be brought to the attention of the federal government. Sometimes I think that in our democratic system we in the federal field forget that there are two other forms of government which are very important to the wellbeing of Canadian citizens. Sometimes we overlook the responsibility that the federal government has to both the provincial and municipal government, but primarily the municipal government. This is why I have proposed this resolution. I am pleased the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) seconded this motion. I know he is vitally interested in this aspect of responsibility in so far as who pays for what is concerned. I do not propose to take too long in making my discourse this afternoon because I know he wants an opportunity to make a few comments in regard to this resolution.
The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of increasing the grants made to municipalities in lieu of property taxes for the use of property by Crown corporations and agencies so that these grants equal the sums paid by private organizations.
The phrase "grants in lieu of taxes" is just a fancy way of saying that the federal government does not pay taxes on real property but, instead, makes arbitrary and unrealistic cash grants to municipal governments. Under Section 125 of the British North America Act, the federal government cannot be taxed by any other level of government. However, since 1877 the federal government has made token payments to towns and cities where it owns land and buildings. These token payments are totally unrelated to the actual tax assessment.
We can take the CBC in Red Deer as an example. The CBC owns and operates broadcasting facilities. In 1980, it paid the county of Red Deer the grand sum of $809.38 as a grant in lieu of taxes. Had the CBC been required to pay the actual property taxes based on assessment, its total bill would have been $4,460. In a nutshell, the county of Red Deer lost over $3,600 on the transaction, yet the municipal government is forced to make available all local services at a loss, I might add. Tenants like that, the county of Red Deer does not actually need.
As a result of the federal government position on paying local taxes, the property tax base of some communities is substantially eroded since the property tax is often the major

October 16, 1981
Municipal Affairs
source of revenue for local authorities. This is the point I wanted to make. These people have a right to be heard.
Large cities such as Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto, Calgary and Edmonton are caught in a tighter vise. Large federal government property holdings represent a considerable loss of potential holdings and represent a considerable loss of potential revenue. In some areas the federal government further impairs revenue generating capabilities of local authorities by precluding or limiting zoning and development. There is no question in my mind that the federal government places unfair burdens on local governments. Because it does not pay its fair share of taxes, the federal government escapes the responsibility of paying its true share of the costs of police and fire protection, sewage disposal and water. I do not mean to say that the taxpayers of Canada will be loaded with any extra taxes. It just means that there will be a more equitable relationship between the levels of government paying the taxes. Because of the federal government, the municipality may also have to undertake expenditures to provide or upgrade roads, schools, and other such facilities to serve the needs of central government employees and their families.
There is no question that the presence of the federal government provides benefits such as jobs, payrolls and new residential property tax bases. But do these benefits offset the fact that the federal government is not a good corporate citizen? In a city such as Ottawa, the shortfall between grants in lieu of taxes and actual assessment runs into the millions. The same is true for many other of our larger cities where the federal government has large holdings. The adequacy of federal contributions has been challenged by local authorities in every region of Canada, especially in Ottawa. Mr. Speaker knows that delegations have appeared before standing committees of the House trying to present their case to the federal government.
The dissatisfaction is based upon three arguments against existing legislation. First, certain properties are excluded from grant calculations such as parks, museums, monuments, etc. This means lost revenue of almost $8 million to the city of Ottawa.
The non-payment of business taxes on federal commercially-assessed properties is the second argument against the existing legislation. The federal government's reply is that it is not a business, it does not compete, it does not engage in profit-seeking activities and it does not generate a business income. I must question this. The CBC in Red Deer certainly competes with other commercially-licensed private broadcasters. Not only do the private broadcasters have to make a contribution to the subsidy going to the CBC, they also make a contribution in taxes because they are totally taxed on their assessed property. Such is not the case with the CBC.
The third argument concerns the deductions from the main grant of amounts representing municipal-type services provided directly by the federal government. In effect, the federal government opts out of municipal services. Other taxpayers do not have this choice. Would there not be chaos if large
companies with their own security forces had the right to opt out of their share of the municipal police force costs?
The present formula is patently unfair and out of touch with reality. There is no question that the federal government has the ability and the resources to pay its fair share and thus become a better corporate citizen and be more responsible to Canadian taxpayers. And pay it should, so that there is equity for all taxpayers, business and residential, in any given municipality. If the federal government expects services to be provided, in fairness it should compensate the municipality. The payments should be prorated to put the federal government on approximately the same footing as other local taxpayers. If this situation is not corrected, the federal government could, if it chose, provide a grant in lieu of taxes to any municipality for PetroCan service stations or any other of its oil properties. This is what happens with the CBC, a Crown corporation. Therefore it could also happen with PetroCan. I am not saying that it will, but it is possible under the present regulations.
If the government is supplying a service to the people that is not provided by any other body, I am not so worried; that is not creating a problem for me. I am concerned, however, when a government facility is in competition with private industry and does not carry its fair share of the tax burden. This is unfair to the taxpayers of Canada, Mr. Speaker. Now is the best time to correct this anomaly before it gets out of hand.
Thank you for allowing me to present this case at this time. Mr. Speaker.

This is a good motion, Mr. Speaker, and one that deserves the full attention of the House. He has said that the federal government is not competing in the marketplace with private enterprise and that it does not want to be considered a business. Is that because it does not do business and does not compete with other private enterprises? I would suggest that is not the real reason. It may be the rationale it uses for not wanting to pay the grant in lieu of taxes but, as the minister said on May 28, 1980, according to a newspaper article, for the federal government to pay business taxes across Canada would cost the government $75 million annually. That is why it does not want to be considered a business, Mr. Speaker, so that it will not have to pay taxes to a local municipality. But who pays, Mr. Speaker? Obviously, the residents of the municipalities have to pay while the federal government gets a free ride.
Unfortunately the minister is not in the House today. He should be, because this private members' motion involves a
October 16, 1981

very important principle which falls square in the middle of his responsibilities. He had promised that a task force would examine this whole area, but an article in the Ottawa Citizen of July 9, 1980 reads in part:
-Cosgrove told the committee the task force would not deal with this question and there was no chance the government would accede to the request anyway, because of fiscal restraint.
The government is really saying, then, that this is not a matter of the merits of the proposal for the federal government to pay grants in lieu of business taxes as a private corporation would, but it is really a matter of fiscal restraint. This is not surprising, however, because when the minister introduced Bill C-4, he saw that the principle of the bill was flawed and he promised that a task force would deal with it. But he never delivered on that promise, Mr. Speaker. He made noises about municipalities being recognized in the Constitution. Why would he do that? It is important that this subject should get an adequate hearing because it involves fundamental principles of democracy. The federal government should not be able to act in an arbitrary, unregulated fashion in a local community. It should be subject to the same laws, regulations and legislative authority as any other resident. If there is one thing that the Liberal government has demonstrated, however, it is its utter petu-lence, arrogance and lack of appreciation of the democratic process.
People are fed up with being run over by this government. People are fed up with the government's misuse of arbitrary authority.
This private member's motion raises a very important subject which deserves serious consideration. It has obviously raised some concerns on this side of the House, although I have yet to see any evidence of real concern on the other side. The matter is important to the individual taxpayer because it means that as long as the federal government gets a free ride in the communities across the country, the local taxpayer has to pay more in property taxes. speakeroldname: Mr. Raymond Savard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subsubtopic: AVAILABILITY OF INCREASING GRANTS IN LIEU OF PROPERTY TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a Notice of Motion tabled on April 30, 1980, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) in Alberta suggested that the House consider the possibility of increasing the grants in lieu of taxes paid by Crown corporations to the Canadian taxation authorities so that these grants equal the taxes paid for buildings owned or used by private organizations. First, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the House that the Canadian government now has one of the best and most comprehensive grant programs in the world, and it has worked very well for over 30 years and that our assistance and advice have been requested many times by other countries who wished to improve their own grant programs. There now exists a consultation procedure between Canadian representatives and our American counterparts. The United States wishes to improve their program by learning more about the operation of our grant program.
Not content to sit back and relax, the government has made a deliberate effort within the last few years to improve our own system even more by developing new legislation, methods and approaches, which will enable us to reinforce not only the relationships between the local and central governments but also the fiscal powers of municipalities. The basic plan of the government for improving the grant program consists in developing a system which will deal essentially with the buildings of federal departments and Crown corporations which provide services as though these buildings were taxable. In the case of Crown corporations whose basic role is not to provide services, the plan is similar except that these corporations will be asked in addition to pay subsidies in lieu of the commercial occupancy tax. The amendments to the grant mechanisms of Crown corporations will be regulated on the one hand by the new Municipal Grants Act, and on the other hand, by the draft regulations on grants paid by Crown corporations, the final version of which is now being prepared.
The Municipal Grants Act of 1980, which was passed by the House on July 17, 1980, and promulgated on December 5, 1980, provides in Section 8 that the governor in council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of the act. Paragraph 8(l)(f) concerns the regulations which will provide for the mechanisms to be used by Crown corporations listed in Schedules III and IV of the act concerning their grant programs in lieu of taxes paid to the various taxation authorities under whose juridiction come the buildings of these corporations. Preparation of the draft regulations on the grants paid by Crown corporations is virtually completed after lenghty consultations and negotiations with the corporations, companies, commissions, boards and orgaizations established to fulfil certain functions for the Canadian government. I expect these regulations to be published shortly in the The Canada

October 16, 1981
Municipal Affairs
Gazette and I trust that those concerned will have enough time to give their comments before they are promulgated.
It would now be appropriate to go back a few years and explain why it was decided at the time to improve the grant in lieu of taxes programs for Crown corporations before promulgation of the new legislation on Crown corporations and the revised Financial Administration Act. Most federal Crown corporations have paid grants in lieu of property taxes since the implementation in 1950 of the grant program for departmental buildings. Instead of paying grants, some of these corporations have in fact paid their property and commercial occupancy taxes directly. Throughout the years, however, a number of complaints have been made concerning the grant practices of certain corporations; in addition, there has been public concern about the differences among the practices of various agencies.
In an order issued in March 1967, the cabinet stated that all federal Crown corporations would have to pay grants for their buildings on a basis generally not less generous than that provided in the Municipal Grants Act for payments related to departmental buildings. There has never been any strict legal obligation for the Crown corporations to comply with this, and the government has been considering establishing a stricter measure.
Mr. Speaker, the Municipal Grants Act of 1980 and the proposed regulation on grants paid by Crown corporations have provided for the review and the streamlining of the procedures followed by Crown corporations with regard to grants and have aligned these procedures on those followed by departments. Therefore, Schedules III and IV of the 1980 act on grants to municipalities were established to include all known Crown corporations. Corporations listed in Schedule III are in general functionally dependent on the Consolidated Revenue Fund and are subject to the guidelines contained in the regulations respecting grants in lieu of property tax or frontage or land tax and the local improvement or development tax. These guidelines are closely modelled on those included in the legislation governing departmental buildings.
Corporations included in Schedule IV usually operate without having to use funds from the Consolidated Revenue Fund and they must not only comply with the guidelines governing grants in lieu of property, frontage or land tax, but they must also pay grants in lieu of business occupancy tax. Crown corporations are divided into two separate schedules, with respect to grants, for a very logical reason.
Certain corporations, namely those listed in Schedule III, are not independent of the federal treasury in the sense that they need Financial assistance from the government to operate and they are not commercial concerns. Generally speaking, those agencies are akin to federal departments since they do
not compete on the market and do not sell goods or services at prices which would provide a return on invested capital. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the National Capital Commission, the National Research Council of Canada and the Northern Canada Power Commission are examples of federal agencies falling into that category. Conversely, the corporations listed in Schedule IV are generally independent of the federal treasury; they may on occasion be required to compete with the private sector and they have to try to make profits. Among the federal agencies included in that category we might mention Air Canada, the Bank of Canada, Eldorado Nuclear Limited and Petro-Canada. The grants paid in lieu of real property tax and business occupancy tax by the corporations listed in Schedule IV put those corporations on roughly the same footing as private sector organizations: the grants are the equivalent of the taxable amounts claimed by the taxing authorities.
Mr. Speaker, it would have been extremely difficult in the past to take stock of the agencies which might have been defined as Crown corporations and to decide which ones ought to pay grants in lieu of the business occupancy tax. For several years, however, a Privy Council Office task force has been hard at work on the problems linked with Crown corporations. The end result of that activity was Bill C-27 on Crown corporations, the purpose of which was to ensure the control, the management and the imputability of Crown corporations by defining them, listing them and classifying them in schedules. The bill was introduced in Parliament in 1979 but, for various reasons, it was not passed. I expect it will be reintroduced in the near future so as to include certain amendments to implement the recommendations made since 1979 which take into account the different status of a certain number of corporations created since then.
The government has decided that even if there were a direct link between the schedules listing the Crown corporations in the new Municipal Grants Act and those included in the new Crown Corporations Act, it would be altogether inappropriate to give to the Municipal Grants Act a basic role with respect to the policy concerning Crown corporations. The new Crown Corporations Act will define that policy and whenever it comes into effect it will contain a reference to Schedules III and IV of the Municipal Grants Act, 1980. That reference will be kept up to date as new Crown corporations are set up or as old corporations are phased out or are reclassified. It is important that any new agency be automatically subjected to the guidelines set out in the Municipal Grants Act. Once the schedules to the proposed new legislation on Crown corporations are firmly established, the Municipal Grants Act, 1980, will finally be amended accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with a view to taking into consideration any amendment made to the schedules and establishing an automatic link between the schedules to both acts.
October 16, 1981

subsubtopic: AVAILABILITY OF INCREASING GRANTS IN LIEU OF PROPERTY TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time that I have had the privilege of participating in a debate in this House since we have come back from the summer adjournment. I do so with some enthusiasm with respect to this particular piece of parliamentary business which is before us.
As the House knows, the wording is quite simple and the resolution is quite simple: that in the opinion of the House, the government should consider the advisability of increasing grants made to municipalities in lieu of property taxes, compensating for the use of property by Crown corporations and agencies, so that these grants should be comparable to the taxes paid by private organizations.
If I followed the parliamentary secretary correctly, he said that in the last little while there has been a vast improvement in the legislative framework within which grants in lieu of taxes are now paid. He is quite right. However, I think it would be very foolish of any of us to assume that the bill that was passed, which was piloted in this House by my seatmate, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), when he was minister of finance, is the last word. I know that the minister of finance at that time did not consider it to be the last word, nor should the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Savard), nor should his minister.
He is as aware as I am that there are a number of things which can be done to improve the position at the moment. I think he is aware of its importance. I know the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) is aware, and I am grateful to him for the privilege of seconding this most worth-while motion. I will not go over the ground, but if the parliamentary secretary speaks to his minister from time to time, I hope he will inform him that there is a great deal to be done in the business tax area. I think we are past the point, at least in terms of the operation of the Canadian government, when it can be argued that the government is not in business. In many ways it is in business. Some would regret it. Some would welcome it, depending on one's philosophy. But there are many aspects of government operations that have about them all the indications of business in the commercial world. They compete in many ways with the commercial world. There are almost 500 Crown agencies that have been identified thus far. There may be more. They are in business in many ways, so that process must go on.
To the extent that those businesses in the name of the Crown are located in some of the 2,000 municipalities across the country that benefit from their presence and from this legislation, it is important that we settle and resolve once and for all the position of the local municipalities with respect to business taxes. They are meant to compensate municipalities for services which are rendered to businesses and agencies of all kinds the costs for which are borne on the backs of the local ratepayers, and to the extent there is not an equitable contri-
Municipal Affairs
bution by government at all levels to that local tax base, those taxpayers have to pay a lot more. It is that balance that we ought to be seeking. I commend that to the parliamentary secretary and I ask him to take that message to his minister.
One other matter recently came up right here with respect to the national capital. It occurred in the House of Commons today. I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) about two decentralization programs, one involving the Post Office and the other involving the ministry of the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox). I gave him an opportunity, first, to deny that it was true that those two agencies were being moved, and, second, to deny that the government was not in fact revitalizing, rejuvenating and reviving the process of decentralization which the former president of the Treasury Board in the Clark government had the good sense to cancel, to the extent that it was reasonably possible to do.
All hon. members will recall our decision to cancel or defer the move of 19 of the agencies that were to move, because of the nature of the service they provided and because of the lack of cost benefit in the move. I supported that decision. As hon. members know, in some cases the process was so far advanced that this could not be done. If this is the case, and if the government is planning on doing that, then the government could affect dramatically the tax base of all municipalities within the national capital region. On both sides of the river we have regional governments. Their taxation is based on a proportionate sharing of the cost of the provision of services. If the tax base is eroded in one municipality, perhaps Ottawa or Hull, then to the extent that funds are necessary to carry the municipal services that have been put in place, other taxpayers have to bear that cost.
I want the government to understand, because I do not intend to let this matter drop, that much more is involved than just physically relocating bodies and work; it has a profound effect on local municipalities. It also has a profound effect on families and a whole host of other things that I will debate at another time. But it does relate to the issue that is still outstanding and unresolved between the municipalities within the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton which I know best, and the federal government. It is something which must be dealt with and cleared up.
We are still not at idem with respect to the amount that is appropriately owed under the existing statutes. The business tax matter is not in it at all. The hon. member for Red Deer says that we owe $8 million in arrears in the city of Ottawa, and that affects all the municipalities around on this side of the river.
The mayor of Ottawa, quite properly, has called for a meeting to settle the issue, to engage representatives of all levels of government in settling the issue. Speaking for myself, I am prepared to go to such a meeting if the minister is prepared to invite us.
The other matter on the horizon bearing on municipal services is the whole question of established program financing. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has indicated that he intends to reduce transfers to the provinces for certain

October 16, 1981
Municipal Affairs
programs and post-secondary education, as well as for social programs, parts of which have a municipal base; all of which arise from the provincial base.
I do not have figures to substantiate this, but I would like someone to show that the general principle is wrong. The general principle that I refer to is that there will be a crimping from the provinces to the local municipalities, to the extent that the provinces are denied those funds heretofore available by transfer from the federal government. The services will have to be provided. The cost will have to be borne somewhere. What will happen? They will be borne to a greater and greater degree on the business taxpayers, and the property taxpayers in the municipalities.
I ask the parliamentary secretary to implore the Minister of Finance, his own minister, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) to take a look at the unanimous report of this Parliament which said that it was wrong for there to be any change in the present basis. To do so at this time would cripple the delivery of services in some areas. That was the unanimous report. That was not the opposition speaking. That was not just the New Democratic Party speaking, it was the Liberal government's own backbenchers speaking as a result of a reference given to them to study the matter, with the approval, I suppose, of the government, and those were their conclusions.
The representatives decided that the program which has been initiated will have an effect on provinces, on municipalities and on taxpayers, and thereby it will have also an effect on renters in all communities. This is a proposition which ought to be avoided and ought not to be advanced by this government. I would ask the parliamentary secretary to take that message to his minister.
It is important, I think, that we recognize that at the root of our system of delivery of services to people are the municipalities. Governments have a duty to pay their way to the fullest extent, not to hide behind constitutional niceties that one Crown cannot tax the other; not to use semantics and nomenclature; not to use the word Crown or the concept of the Crown to sneak out of or to get away from obligations which are owed by virtue of service. I hope we are moving in that direction.
The parliamentary secretary has raised the question in terms of the goodness of the program. He said that other countries are looking at us, that we have a good program, I do not doubt that at all. I am proud of it and if we are leaders in that field, then it is a feather in our caps. All of us should be pleased about that. But I must add this caveat, that we have not yet reached the end of the road.
I think we should take a look at a number of government programs, such as, for example, the Canadian Oil Substitution Program, which is of interest to municipalities. I am a supp-porter of that program. I think it is a good idea to get people off using oil if we can, and on to using something else. But many cities in Canada, many municipalities in the country, have programs for the renovation of various schools and public facilities. One of the principal motives behind these programs is the conservation of energy. I am sure if hon. members asked
many municipal leaders, they would say quite frankly that they would like to substitute oil based equipment with gas or electrically based alternatives as far as possible.
I was quite stunned to see a letter from the head of a municipality in the national capital region in fact it was the Mayor of Ottawa-saying that she had made inquiries with the Renewable Energy Secretariat of Energy, Mines and Resources Canada, and with the Ontario minister of industry and found that municipalities or their agencies were not entitled to apply for a grant under that grant program of conversion. The reason being, of course, that it is a tax-incentive program designed for private individuals and corporations.
It seems to me it would be helpful to municipalities-if we are talking about grants generally, and this has been the subject of this debate-if the parliamentary secretary suggested to the minister of energy that they re-examine that program to see whether the tremendous users of energy might not have grants given to them to entice them to change, so they would in fact have some incentive to help the government in its own energy conservation program, a program in which all Canadians should be engaged. I understand that is not the case at the moment. I commend that as one proposition the parliamentary secretary might take to his minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). In terms of municipalities, I think it would be helpful to the government's program of conservation if that proposition could be advanced.
I regard the resolution as important not just to the City of Ottawa, and not just to municipalities within the national capital region, but to the 2,000 of them in the country. There are post offices everywhere and public buildings of all kinds in municipalities. Even if we have the best system thus far, and I am not going to dispute that today, the parliamentary secretary knows, as his speech implied, that there are areas in which it could be improved.
I commend the hon. member for Red Deer for allowing us to debate this matter in order that we could bring to the attention of the ministry and the government the support there would be in this House of Commons on all sides for improvement to the present system. The basis of our democracy is a healthy, strong local government, and the statute with regard to grants in lieu of taxes is important. The contribution of the federal government to the welfare of people living in these municipalities could be made even more significant by some improvement to the system, perfect as it is now.

subsubtopic: AVAILABILITY OF INCREASING GRANTS IN LIEU OF PROPERTY TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the notice of motion of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), may I remind him that it has already been suggested that the program providing grants in lieu of property taxes for the use of property by Crown corporations and agencies should apply not only to property taxes but also to business occupancy taxes. First of all, I should like to go back to the origins of the municipal business
October 16, 1981

occupancy tax, and then show why the federal administration feels that only some designated Crown corporations should pay Canadian tax authorities grants in lieu of taxes.
Mr. Speaker, going back to the turn of the century, we find that in fact the only source of revenue available to municipalities for financing local services was property taxes. Even then, it was obvious that unless they could find new sources of revenue, local governments could not afford the expenditures needed to increase and improve their services.
As time went on, Mr. Speaker, the federal government and the provinces made studies and set up commissions entrusted with looking into the matter. Generally, the resulting reports stressed the need for municipal authorities to levy an additional tax on the capital or rental value of buildings occupied by financial or business companies, that is, a special tax levied by the municipality on properties used for business purposes I repeat, for business purposes. That tax is justifiable for the following reason: When someone can reasonably expect to make a gain or profit by carrying out a commercial activity in a municipality and by supplying the risk capital required and the know-how, but when in fact he also benefits from local services, facilities, labour, transportation services as well as the purchasing power of the municipality, it is only fair then that he should pay out an additional amount to municipal coffers just for the privilege of benefiting from a large number of the elements necessary for making a profit.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot dispute the fact that the term "commercial operation" refers to a gainful occupation, a craft, a profession, a function or any other activity performed more or less continuously with a view to making a profit. It is a concise definition drawn from precedents dealing with the assessment of taxation in Canada. It is also a definition which apparently includes some criteria or basic principles. It has been noted that some Crown corporations which are operating without relying on the Treasury, will have to pay a commercial occupancy tax when it comes into effect. In order to justify the payment of such a tax on the federal buildings or Crown corporations listed in Schedule III of the new legislation on municipal subsidies we would have either explicitly or implicitly to equate the services of the federal government with those of a commercial operation. Now such an equation is totally unfounded. These departments and corporations are service-oriented and not profit-oriented, and thus one cannot consider them as carrying out a commercial activity in the conventional sense.
In Canada, Mr. Speaker, the great majority of municipalities and provincial governments do not pay any business occupancy tax on the properties owned by them or managed by corporations, organizations or councils created by them, except for those which are specifically profit-seeking, such as hydroelectric commissions or provincial liquor stores. However, one should note that the province of Quebec has innovated by establishing a program which, since 1980, calls for the pay-
Municipal Affairs
ment to municipalities of grants in lieu of business occupancy taxes and property taxes on almost every property owned by its departments and Crown corporations. Because of the close financial links between the provincial and municipal administrations, the province is able to cancel or to roll back other forms of financial aid. This possibility does not exist quite in the same degree in the case of the federal government.
The business occupancy tax does not apply in several areas of Canada. Also, there are many ways to determine its rate. It may be a fixed percentage of the annual amount of rental revenues or a fixed amount, or else a percentage of the assessment. Since this percentage is different depending on the type of business activity, in some cases a provincial statute makes the payment of the business occupancy tax mandatory. In other cases, provisions stipulate that the tax becomes payable only on the request of the city council. In the latter case, were the Canadian government to decide to pay such taxes on departmental or Crown corporation property, city councils would no doubt tend to take advantage of that option, especially in cases where such holdings make up most of the landed property in the municipality.
There are two other very significant factors for not paying business occupancy taxes on Canadian Crown buildings. First the disparity of amounts that would be distributed across Canada, and second, the cost to the federal treasury in these days of budgetary restraint. Firstly, Mr. Speaker, were grants in lieu of business occupancy taxes to be paid, widely unequal amounts would be distributed across Canada since 80 per cent of the Canadian federal property holdings come under less than 5 per cent of the taxing authorities receiving grants. This being the case, it seemed preferable to extend the scope of the grant program by increasing the categories of buildings, entitled, and therefore the amount of grants paid to a number of municipalities that until now were receiving minimal or no grants.

Further, if grants in lieu of business occupancy taxes were to be paid on all federal Crown property, huge amounts of money would be involved. The over-all cost would be extremely difficult to accurately assess, but it might very well total $100 million, that is $85 million for departmental buildings and $15 for Crown corporation buildings listed in Schedule III. In summary, Mr. Speaker, and I conclude on this, it is simply impossible to incur such expenditures.

I would like to second the remarks made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) and the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) who argued the points raised in this motion extremely well. This is very important to all members who have federal land holdings in their constituency.

October 16, 1981
Municipal Affairs
I would like to refer specifically to one type of federal property often found in municipalities. That is, land reserved for the Indians. There are two types of land reserved for Indians. One is Indian reserves under the Indian Act. In my constituency there are a number of cases in which the reserves are actually located within municipalities. There is need for improvement of the financial arrangements between the Government of Canada, presumably acting on behalf of the people who live on the reserve, and the municipality called upon to provide services for that reserve. The greatest problem lies in those areas of land designated as land reserved for Indians but not for Indian reserves. This may sound peculiar but that is the wording of the legislation. I know a couple of municipalities which have several acres of designated land reserved for Indians but not for Indian reserves. The Government of Canada pays grants in lieu of taxes to the municipality. However, since those areas of land have not been legally subdivided, although those areas have been built upon and people live there, the government will only pay grants in lieu of taxes as if the land were completely undeveloped. The result is very small revenue accruing to the local municipal governments. For that reason, they have taken the attitude that they are not responsible for the provision of full services to those areas because there is no revenue comirtg into the municipality.
I think this matter should be looked into by the government. It should be rectified in some way.
Having brought this matter to the attention of the House, I am prepared to let the hon. member from the New Democratic Party speak before we vote on this important motion.

subsubtopic: AVAILABILITY OF INCREASING GRANTS IN LIEU OF PROPERTY TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in this debate, although I have only five minutes to speak on such a detailed matter that would require half an hour. I believe that if all government agencies and Crown corporations were to pay grants equal to the amount of taxes paid by private agencies in the various areas of Canada, it would mean these agencies and corporations not only would still have to pay the full amount of grants for their lands and buildings as they now have to, but also grants in lieu of business occupancy taxes. The previous speaker dealt with the business occupancy tax, and indicated the very valid reasons why that tax should not apply. I now intend to show why it is appropriate to exclude from their grant programs building units owned by them, in the same way those units are excluded from departmental grants applicable to property holdings.
The only class of facilities which might be included without giving rise to considerable pressure for the inclusion of other
classes in the grant program would be machinery and equipment. However, the arguments raised against grants for facilities are equally valid for machinery and equipment, including the very erratic way in which the latter are taxed or not taxed in the various areas of Canada when they are owned by the business community of the private sector.
Now, machinery raises administrative problems due to the fact that certain types of equipment are part of buildings. According to the general principle applied, even if a piece of machinery may be within a building and fixed to it, it is not considered to be part of that building, except if it is used in some way in its operation like, for instance, elevators, escalators, boilers, plumbing systems, air conditioning units, sprinklers, etc., which are all considered to be part of the building and are liable for grants in the case of buildings owned by Crown corporations or government departments.
Notwithstanding the different ways in which these matters are dealt with by individual provinces, the various types of buildings are not all taxed when they belong to the private sector. In this context and in view of the difficulties which might stem from the payment of grants on some buildings in some provinces and the non-payment of grants on similar facilities in other provinces, something which might jeopardize the universal nature of the grants program, it was felt that all Crown constructions had to be excluded.
This firm position concerning facilities is based on several other reasons. First of all, if one type of property were included in the grant scheme, there would be strong pressures, for other types to be subjected to the scheme, for it does not seem logical to include some while excluding others. Also, if all facilities were to give rise to grants, Crown corporations would have to agree, for this is provided for under Section 8(1 )(f) of the 1980 legislation. This decision would prove very costly to a number of Crown corporations to the point where they could no longer meet their obligations.
On the other hand, and this has nothing to do strictly speaking with facilities, few people are aware that under the grants program administered by the federal government, grants are paid in respect of some classes of buildings which would not be taxed were they to belong to other organizations. I should mention, by way of conclusion, schools, hospitals, penitentiaries, fire halls, etc.
